beats.text: Kinematics told us where the joints should be. Dynamics asks how hard the motors must work to get them there.
Start with one joint, a pendulum. With the motor off, gravity alone swings it.
Its equation is Newton's second law, for rotation: inertia times angular acceleration, plus the gravity torque, equals the motor torque.
A whole robot obeys the same law, with one row per joint.
M is the mass matrix. It changes with the arm's pose.
C holds the Coriolis and centrifugal effects, which appear when several joints move at once.
g is gravity: the torque needed just to hold the arm up.
And tau, on the right, is what the motors apply.
This one equation answers two different questions.
Forward dynamics: given the torques, how will the robot move? We solve for the acceleration, then integrate over time. That is what a physics simulator does.
Inverse dynamics: to move like this, what torques do I need? Just plug the motion in and multiply. That is what a robot controller does, a thousand times a second.
Here is forward dynamics. The motors are off, so tau is zero.
Every tiny time step, the simulator solves for the acceleration and integrates it into velocity and angle.
The arm falls, and with no friction it never settles. The motion is chaotic.
Now the reverse. We want the hand to trace this circle, so we compute the torques for that motion, and apply them.
The bars split the shoulder torque into its three terms. At this speed, gravity is the biggest one.
Now the circle runs twice as fast.
The inertia term grows about four times, because acceleration grows with speed squared. The gravity term does not change: it only depends on the pose.
In a real robot, both directions run together.
The controller uses inverse dynamics to turn the desired motion into torques. The robot, or the simulator, is forward dynamics: physics answering back.
Sensors measure the result, and the loop repeats.
Two takeaways: cancel just gravity, and the arm feels weightless. And faster moves cost much more torque.
